dialog.body: Public Works, this is Denise. You caught me on the late shift, what can I do for you?
Yeah, hi. I'm calling about the drain at the corner by our house. Again. I figured I'd get a machine at this hour, honestly.
Nope, you got a person. Which address are we talking about?

Eighteen Howard Street. Fifth Ward. The storm drain right at the corner there backs up every time it rains hard, and our basement floods. My son called yesterday, my husband called back in January, and I'm calling now because I don't know what else to do.
Okay. Can I get your name?
Nilza Pina. P-I-N-A. My husband's Nilson.
Pina, Howard Street. Hold on, let me pull it up. [pause] Okay, yeah, I've got it. I actually think I took your husband's call in January. Middle of the morning, the Monday after that coastal storm?
That sounds right. So you know. You know this isn't new.
I see it, yeah. January twelfth, drain backup at the corner, and a crew went out the next day, the thirteenth.
They went out, sure. They cleaned off the grate. Shoveled some sand and junk out of the top of it and left. That's it. Nobody looked down inside. And now look where we are.
The note says they cleared the grate and took the silt out around the basin. Doesn't say anything about the line itself.

Because they didn't touch the line. My husband watched them. Twenty minutes, maybe. And then this weekend, Saturday night into Sunday, the whole street's a lake again and we've got five inches of water in the basement. Five. In January it was two. So it's getting worse, not better.
Five inches. Okay. So this is the second time this winter.

Second time this winter. Two times in six weeks. And you know what I spent the end of January doing? Hauling stuff out of there. File boxes of paperwork, soaked through. I'm a bookkeeper, those were records. My husband's workbench, his hand tools, half of them rusted. We threw all that out already. We dried it, we sorted it, we threw out what couldn't be saved. And now I'm supposed to do it all again? I'm not doing it again. I'm tired of doing it.
I hear you. That's a lot of work twice.
It's not just work. It's the whole weekend gone. My son was down there Sunday morning with a wet vac before he even had coffee. That's when he called you people.
Right, I see his call too. Wilson? Sunday morning, around ten.

Yes. And what did they tell him? A crew on Tuesday. Tuesday. It's Monday night. If it rains tomorrow morning, before Tuesday whenever, what then? I want somebody out there now. Tonight, tomorrow first thing, I don't care. Check that drain and clear it out. The whole thing, not just the top.

So here's where it stands. The crew is booked for tomorrow, Tuesday the twenty-fourth. That's on the schedule. Tonight I don't have anybody on for a non-emergency drain, but the forecast's dry through tomorrow, so you're not looking at more water before they get there.
Dry. Okay. They said dry before the January one too, and then it came up the street like a river.

Fair. What I can do is put a note on tomorrow's work order that this is a repeat, that the grate was already cleared in January and it backed up anyway, so they need to look at the line under the corner, not just the top. That way they're not walking up and doing the same twenty minutes.
Yeah. Do that. Write it in big letters.
I'm writing it. [pause] 'Second backup this winter, five inches in basement, January visit cleared grate only, check and clear line.' That good?

That's good. But that's tomorrow. What about after tomorrow? Because they're going to come, they're going to poke at it, and then the next storm comes and we're right back here. I want to know is anybody ever going to actually fix this. Like a real fix. Not a guy with a shovel.

That's more of an engineering question than a crew question. Your son's call already has a supervisor calling back by Wednesday. I can flag your file for engineering too, so somebody's looking at whether that corner needs more than a cleaning.

Flag it. Flag everything. Because I'll be honest with you, I'm done being nice about it. My husband's been in this house thirty-eight years. Thirty-eight years. And now twice in one winter? Something changed with that drain, and the city should know what. If nothing happens this time, I'm calling a lawyer. I mean it. I already looked one up.
Understood. I'll put down that you want a permanent fix looked at, and that you're not satisfied with the January visit.
You can put down that I said lawyer, too. I don't care.
I'll note that you're considering legal action. That's your right.
Thank you. [pause] Sorry. It's not you. You picked up the phone, which is more than I expected.
It's alright. Nobody's calling here at six-thirty on a Monday because they're having a good day.

No. I'm sitting here at the kitchen table trying to figure out what we lost this time. I had the insurance stuff up on my e-reader, the screen's cracked right across the middle, but it still works. Kind of like everything in this house right now. Still works, barely.
Was anything else down there this time? For the file.

The spare refrigerator. It's sitting in five inches of water, I don't know if it's done or not. The rest we'd already cleared out after January, that's the only reason we didn't lose more. Everything that was down there is either gone or up on blocks now.
Okay. Spare fridge. Got it.

And there's one more thing. Before the next storm. Whenever they say something big's coming, can somebody call us? Like put us on a list. So we know, so somebody checks that drain before it hits instead of after. I'd rather move things around Friday than vacuum water out Sunday.
I can put that request on the file. I'll put it in as a callback before forecast storms and a pre-storm check on that basin. Best number for that?
Four oh one, five five five, oh one three one. That's the cell. My husband and I share it, so whoever answers.
Four oh one, five five five, zero one three one. Same one your husband gave in January, looks like.
Yeah, it's the same. We're not hard to find.

Alright. So, to read it back to you. Crew's still on for tomorrow, Tuesday, and I added the note to check the line under the corner, not just the grate. Supervisor callback by Wednesday, and I've added your name to it, so they'll want to talk to you too, not just Wilson. Flagged for engineering to look at a permanent fix. And a request for a call and a check before the next big storm.
And the part about the January crew only doing the top.
That's in there. First thing they'll see.
Okay. [pause] Do you know what time tomorrow?

The crews usually start their routes around seven, and repeat backups tend to go out in the morning. So somewhere before lunch is my guess. If it slides, the supervisor call Wednesday is where you'd hear why.
Before lunch. My husband works nights, he'll be up by then. He'll go out and watch them. He'll make sure they look down in there this time.
That's not a bad idea, honestly. He can point out where the water comes up from.
Oh, he'll point. Believe me.
Anything else I can add tonight?
No. Just, if they come tomorrow and do the same thing as last time, I'm calling back. And it won't be you I'm yelling at, but I'm calling back.
Then call back. Ask for the repeat file on Howard Street, it's all in one place now.
Fine. Thank you, Denise. Goodnight.
Goodnight, Mrs. Pina. Get some rest if you can.
